turns.prompt_text: I have a general electric dishwasher here and it's stuck on a rinse. They won't do anything else. I wonder if it's not closing properly
turns.response_html:
A dishwasher stuck mid-cycle—especially on a rinse—is incredibly frustrating, but you are hitting on a very likely culprit right out of the gate. If the control board doesn't get a definitive signal that the door is completely latched and sealed, it will refuse to progress the cycle or accept new commands as a safety precaution.

Before you pull the whole machine out, let’s run through a quick diagnostic checklist to see if we can get it unstuck, starting with that door latch.

1. Check the Door Latch & Microswitches

Even if the door feels like it's closed, the internal switches might not be registering.

  • The Physical Latch: Open the door and inspect the latch assembly at the top center of the door. Look into the catch hole on the underside of the countertop/frame. Is there debris, a stray piece of silverware, or a broken plastic piece blocking the strike plate?
  • The Switch Test: When you close the door, do you hear a distinct, mechanical "click"? If it closes softly without that definitive click, the microswitches inside the latch housing might be misaligned or dead.
  • Door Gasket: Check the black rubber seal around the tub. If it has slipped out of its groove near the top, it can prevent the door from pushing in those last few millimeters required to trip the sensor.

2. Force a Hard Reset (Clear the Stuck Brain)

GE dishwashers are notorious for getting their control boards stuck in a loop when a cycle is interrupted. You need to force it to clear its memory.

  • The Key Dance: Press and hold the Start/Reset button for about 3 to 5 seconds. On most GE models, this will force the dishwasher into a 2-minute pump-out cycle. You should hear the drain pump kick on. Wait for the flashing lights to stop.
  • Kill the Power: If the control panel is completely locked up and won't respond to the reset button, go to your home's breaker box and flip the breaker for the dishwasher Off. Leave it off for a full 5 minutes to let the capacitors on the control board completely drain. Flip it back on and see if the panel has reset to normal.

3. Other Sneaky Culprits

If the door is definitely closing tightly and a reset doesn't work, a couple of other things can cause a GE dishwasher to hang up on a rinse cycle:

  • The Flood Switch / Float Switch: There is a small plastic float dome on the bottom floor of the dishwasher tub. If it's stuck in the "up" position (perhaps because a piece of food or a bone got wedged under it), the dishwasher thinks it is overflowing and will continuously run the drain/rinse routine while blocking any other cycle from starting. Give it a gentle tap to make sure it bobs up and down freely.
  • Heating Element Failure: Some older GE cycles will pause and wait indefinitely if the water isn't reaching a specific temperature during certain cycle phases. If the heating element at the bottom is burned out (look for cracks or white blistering on the loop), the timer will just sit there waiting for heat that is never coming.

What to try first:

Give that Start/Reset button a long hold, and if that fails, kill the breaker. While the power is off, inspect the door strike plate to make sure it isn't loose or bent.

When you try to close it or run a reset, do any specific lights on the panel flash, or is it completely unresponsive to button presses?

turns.prompt_text: I have a bunch of bottles with labels on them. I want to get the labels off. I've tried soaking them in warm water and soap and then I put some lemon juice in and let it continue to soak I also have baking soda I could try
turns.response_html:
You are already on the right track! The reason warm water and dish soap didn't completely do the trick is that most bottle labels use oil-based, pressure-sensitive adhesives. Soap and water are great for water-soluble glues (like on wine bottles), but for tough sticker residue, you need something that breaks down the oil.

Since you have baking soda, you have the perfect secret weapon. When you mix it with a little oil, it creates a paste that breaks down the adhesive while providing a gentle abrasive to scrub it away.

Here is how to deploy what you have on hand to get those labels completely off:

The Baking Soda & Oil Method

The best approach for stubborn, plastic, or metallic labels.

  1. Peel what you can: Since you've already soaked them, try to peel away the top layer of paper or plastic. If only the sticky, gooey residue is left, perfect.
  2. Make the paste: Mix equal parts baking soda and any cooking oil you have in the kitchen (vegetable oil, olive oil, or canola oil all work great). You want a thick, gritty paste.
  3. Apply and wait: Rub the paste generously over the sticky parts of the bottles. Let it sit for 15 to 20 minutes. The oil penetrates and softens the glue, while the lemon juice you already used helps cut through the slick layer.
  4. Scrub it down: Take a scrubby sponge or an old cloth and rub in a circular motion. The baking soda acts as a mild abrasive, lifting the glue without scratching the glass.
  5. Wash off the oil: Wash the bottles one last time with warm water and dawn/dish soap to cut the greasy film left by the oil.

Why the Lemon Juice Didn't Quite Finish the Job

Lemon juice contains citric acid, which is excellent for breaking down certain mineral deposits or water-based glues (and it's a fantastic natural cleaner for glass surfaces), but it lacks the oil-dissolving chemistry needed for heavy-duty sticker adhesives. By pairing the acid treatment they already got with an oil-and-baking-soda paste, you are attacking the glue from both chemical angles.

Give the baking soda and oil paste a shot on one of the bottles—it usually rolls the adhesive right off in clumps!
